column2: I bow to Govinda, the supreme bliss, the true teacher, who is the goal of the conclusions of all the Vedanta, yet beyond the reach of the senses.

Having somehow gained a human birth, so hard to get, and in it manhood and thorough learning in the scriptures — the fool who does not strive for liberation of the Self kills himself by clinging to what is unreal.
Who then is more foolish than one who is careless of his own good, having obtained this rare human body and in it manhood?

Let them recite the scriptures, worship the gods, perform rites, and pray to the deities — without the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, liberation is not attained even in a hundred Brahma-lifetimes.
There is no hope of immortality through wealth, says the scripture, clearly showing that works are no cause of liberation.

Therefore the wise man should strive for liberation, having renounced the desire for pleasure in outer objects; approaching a good and great teacher, and with his mind concentrated on the meaning taught by him,
let him lift up his self by the Self, sunk in the ocean of worldly existence, by attaining steadfastness in yoga and devotion to right vision.
Renouncing all works, for release from the bonds of worldly existence, let the wise and steadfast strive, devoted to the practice of the Self.
Work is for the purification of the mind, not for the perception of the Reality; the Reality is established by inquiry, not even a little by crores of works.
The ascertainment of the truth of the rope is accomplished by right inquiry, and it destroys the fear and pain caused by the great snake that arose from delusion.
The determination of a matter is seen to come through inquiry and wholesome advice — not by bathing, nor by giving, nor by a hundred breath-controls.
The attainment of the fruit especially requires one who is qualified; place, time and the like are the helpers in this.
Therefore inquiry into the reality of the Self is to be made by the seeker, approaching a teacher who is an ocean of compassion and the best of the knowers of Brahman.
A person who is intelligent, learned, skilled in argument and counter-argument, and marked by the characteristics stated, is qualified for the knowledge of the Self.
One who is discriminating, dispassionate, endowed with the qualities beginning with calmness, and who longs for liberation alone, is considered fit for the inquiry into Brahman.
Four means have been named here by the wise: only when they exist is steadfastness possible, and in their absence it is not accomplished.

First is reckoned the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal; then dispassion for enjoying results here and hereafter; then the six-fold wealth beginning with calmness; and the longing for liberation — clearly so.
The firm conviction "Brahman is real, the world is unreal" — this is called the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal.
That is dispassion: the desire to give up, arising from seeing, hearing and the like, and revulsion toward all perishable objects of enjoyment from the body up to Brahma's world.
Having turned away from the multitude of objects of enjoyment by repeatedly seeing their faults, the mind's steady abiding on its own goal is called calmness (shama).

Turning both kinds of senses away from their objects and placing them in their own seats is called self-control (dama); the mind's not depending on external things is the highest withdrawal (uparati).
Bearing all sorrows without seeking to redress them, and free from worry and lament — this is called forbearance (titiksha).
Firm acceptance, as true, of what the scriptures and the teacher say — this the good call faith (shraddha), by which the Reality is attained.
Constant, right placing of the intellect on pure Brahman is called concentration (samadhana), not the indulging of the mind.
The wish to free oneself, through knowledge of one's own nature, from the bonds — from ego down to the body — that are imagined through ignorance, is the longing for liberation (mumukshuta).
Even if weak or moderate, this (longing), strengthened by dispassion, calmness and the like and by the teacher's grace, bears fruit.
In one in whom dispassion and the longing for liberation are intense, calmness and the rest become meaningful and fruitful.
Where these two — dispassion and longing for liberation — are weak, calmness and the rest are a mere appearance, like water in a desert.
Among the means to liberation devotion is greatest; the constant seeking of one's own true nature is called devotion.

Others say that devotion is the seeking of the truth of one's own Self. One who is endowed with the means described, and who wishes to know the truth of the Self, should approach a wise teacher, from whom release from bondage comes.

(Such a teacher is) one learned in the Vedas, sinless, unstruck by desire, the best of the knowers of Brahman, resting in Brahman, tranquil like a fire without fuel, an ocean of causeless compassion, a friend of the good who bow to him.
Having worshipped that teacher with devotion, by humility, respect and service, and having approached him when he is pleased, let him ask what is to be known of the Self.

Master, homage to you, friend of those who bow, ocean of compassion — I have fallen into the sea of worldly existence. Lift me up with your own glance, showering the nectar of your straight and great compassion.
Scorched by the unquenchable forest-fire of worldly existence, shaken by the winds of adverse fortune, afraid, I have come to you. Protect me from death; I know no other refuge.
Peaceful, great, good people live (in the world) like spring, doing good to all; having themselves crossed the dreadful ocean of existence, they without any cause help others across too.
This is the very nature of the great: to remove the toil of others. The moon itself, indeed, protects the earth scorched by the harsh rays of the sun.

With the nectar of your words — purified, cool, soothing to hear, poured from the vessel of your speech, and imbued with the experience of the taste of Brahman's bliss — sprinkle me, O Lord, who am scorched by the flames of the forest-fire of worldly suffering. Blessed are those who, by even a moment of your glance, have been made fit and accepted.
How shall I cross this ocean of existence? What is my way, what means is there? I know nothing. Protect me out of compassion, Lord, and end the suffering of worldly life.
Seeing him thus speaking, taking refuge, scorched by the heat of the forest-fire of worldly existence, the great soul, with a glance moist with compassion, should at once give him freedom from fear.
That wise one should, out of compassion alone, teach the truth to the seeker who has come to him, who longs for liberation, does as instructed, has a tranquil mind and is endowed with calmness.
Do not fear, O wise one; there is no danger for you. There is a way to cross the sea of worldly existence; I shall show you the very path by which the ascetics have gone to its farther shore.
There is a great means that destroys the fear of worldly existence; by it you will cross the ocean of existence and attain supreme bliss.
From inquiry into the meaning of the Vedanta arises the highest knowledge; by that follows the final destruction of the suffering of worldly existence.

The scripture itself declares the causes of liberation for the seeker: faith, devotion, meditation and yoga. Whoever abides in these, his liberation comes from the bondage of the body imagined through ignorance.

Through ignorance, your Supreme Self is bound to the not-Self, and from that alone comes transmigration. The fire of knowledge, arisen from discrimination between the two, burns up the effect of ignorance together with its root.
The disciple said: "Master, please listen; I ask this question, on hearing the answer to which from your mouth I shall have fulfilled my purpose."

What is bondage? How has it come? How does it persist? How is there release from it? What is the not-Self? What is the Supreme Self? And how is the distinction between the two made? Please tell me this.
The venerable teacher said: "You are blessed, your purpose is fulfilled, and your family is made pure by you, since you wish to become Brahman by release from the bond of ignorance."
Sons and others can discharge a father's debts; but no one other than oneself can release oneself from bondage.
The suffering of one carrying a load on his head can be removed by others, but the suffering caused by hunger and the like cannot be removed by anyone except oneself.
A patient follows a healthy diet and takes medicine himself; the cure is seen for him, not through what others do.
The nature of the Reality is to be known by oneself through the eye of clear knowledge, not by a scholar. The form of the moon must be known by one's own eyes; can it be understood through others?
Who, except the Self, could loosen the bonds of ignorance, desire, action and the rest, even in hundreds of crores of ages?
Not by yoga, not by Sankhya, not by works, and not by learning, but by the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is liberation achieved, not otherwise.
The beauty of the lute's form and the skill of playing its strings only please people; they do not lead to sovereignty.
Fluent speech, a shower of words, and skill in expounding the scriptures — such scholarship of scholars is for enjoyment, not for liberation.
When the Supreme Reality is not known, the study of scriptures is fruitless; and when the Supreme Reality is known, the study of scriptures is also fruitless.
A net of words is a great forest that causes the mind to wander; therefore the knowers of the Reality should, with effort, know the truth of the Self.
For one bitten by the snake of ignorance, what use are Vedas, scriptures, mantras or medicines, without the medicine of the knowledge of Brahman?
A disease does not go merely by the word 'medicine' without drinking it; without direct experience, one is not liberated by the words 'Brahman'.
Without dissolving the visible world and without knowing the truth of the Self, how can there be liberation for men by mere words, whose only fruit is talk?
Without destroying enemies and without acquiring the wealth of the whole earth, one does not become a king by saying 'I am a king.'

As buried treasure requires trustworthy words, digging, the lifting away of the stones above, and acceptance (taking it up), and does not come out by mere outer words — so the pure truth of the Self, hidden by the effect of illusion, is gained through the teaching of a knower of Brahman, reflection and meditation, and not by wrong reasonings.
Therefore, for release from the bonds of worldly existence, the wise should make effort by themselves, as in a disease and the like.

The question you have asked today, like (a question about) a disease and the like, is excellent, approved by knowers of the scriptures, agreed upon, brief in form and of deep meaning, and it is to be known by seekers of liberation.
Listen attentively, wise one, to what I now say; by hearing it you will at once be freed from the bonds of worldly existence.
The first cause of liberation is said to be extreme dispassion toward perishable things; then calmness, self-control, forbearance, and thorough renunciation of all the works one is engaged in.

Then hearing the scripture, reflection, and long, constant, unbroken meditation on the truth by the sage; then, attaining the supreme undifferentiated state, the wise one obtains the bliss of liberation right here.
What you now need to know is the discrimination between the Self and the not-Self; I shall tell it fully — hear it and fix it in yourself.
This (body) is composed of the substances called marrow, bone, fat, flesh, blood, skin and cuticle, and furnished with feet, thighs, chest, arms, back, head, and limbs and sub-limbs.
The body, known as 'I' and 'mine', the seat of delusion, is called by the wise the gross body. Space, air, fire, water and earth are the subtle elements.
Mixed with parts of one another, they become gross and are the causes of the gross body; their fine measures, sound and the other five, are the objects, for the pleasure of the enjoyer.
The deluded who are bound to these objects by the strong, hard-to-subdue cord of attachment go and come, down and up, carried swiftly by the messenger of their own karma.
By the five — sound and the rest — five (creatures) have met death, each bound by its own quality: deer, elephant, moth, fish and bee. What then of a man, seized by all five?
The objects are worse in fault than the poison of a black snake: poison kills only the one who takes it, but this (the object) kills even the one who merely looks at it with his eyes.
He who is freed from the great noose of desire for objects, so hard to give up, alone is fit for liberation, and no other, even one who knows the six systems.

For seekers of liberation who have only a passing dispassion and are trying to reach the farther shore of the ocean of existence, the crocodile of desire seizes them by the throat midway and drags them back by force.
He who has slain the crocodile called the object with the sword of true dispassion crosses the ocean of worldly existence free from obstacles.

Know that for one of unclear mind who walks along the rough paths of objects, death approaches at every step; but for one who walks by the words of good and wise teachers and by his own reason, know that success comes truly.

If you have a desire for liberation, shun sense-objects from afar like poison, and always with reverence cultivate, like nectar, contentment, compassion, forgiveness, straightforwardness, tranquillity and self-control.

Whoever, giving up what must be done every moment for freedom from the bonds made by beginningless ignorance, is intent on nourishing this body — which exists for the sake of another — kills himself thereby.
He who, intent on nourishing the body, wishes to see the Self, is like one who seizes a crocodile, thinking it a log, in order to cross the river.
Delusion about the body and the like is the great death of the seeker of liberation. He who has conquered delusion is fit for the state of liberation.
Conquer delusion, the great death, about body, wife, children and the like; having conquered it, the sages reach that supreme abode of Vishnu.
This gross body, a mass of skin, flesh, blood, sinew, fat, marrow and bone, full of urine and excrement, is contemptible.

This gross body, produced from the gross elements after their fivefold combination, through past actions, is the abode of the Self's enjoyment. Its state is the waking state, in which gross objects are experienced.
The soul, by the outer senses, serves gross objects of many kinds — garlands, sandal paste, women and the like — and does it all by itself; therefore the body is praised in the waking state.
Know this gross body to be the house of the Person, on which the whole outer world depends, as a house is to a householder.

Birth, decay and death are properties of the gross body, and so are stoutness and many other conditions like childhood, the rules of castes and stages of life, the many diseases, and the special modes of worship, disrespect and honour.
The organs of knowledge are ear, skin, eye, nose and tongue, because they make objects known; the organs of action are speech, hands, feet, anus and genital, because they are prone to act.
The inner organ, called mind, intellect, ego and memory, is named by its functions: the mind by will and doubt, the intellect by its property of determining objects,
the ego by identification ('I') in these, and the memory by its property of seeking its own aims.
It is breath, which becomes prana, apana, vyana, udana and samana, by the difference of its functions, as gold and water take different forms.

The five organs of speech and the rest, the five organs of hearing and the rest, the five breaths, the five elements beginning with space, intellect and the rest, ignorance, desire and action — these eight (groups) they call the subtle body.

Hear now the body called subtle, the linga, produced from the unmixed elements, bearing its impressions, experiencing the fruit of actions — the beginningless, ignorance-caused limiting adjunct of the Self.

The dream is this (subtle body's) distinct state, in which it shines with only itself as remainder; in dream the intellect itself, in the waking manner, through the impressions of many kinds of times,

appears as agent and the rest, and shines; there the Supreme Self shines by itself — self-luminous, having the intellect alone as its limiting adjunct, the witness of all, untouched by the faint traces of actions done by it — unattached, therefore untouched by any action done through the adjunct.
This subtle body is the instrument of all activity of the Self, the Person of consciousness, like the carpenter's adze and the like; by it, the Self remains unattached.
